top_choice_rationale: P001 credits Katori and Ye for the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock, a single idea (cancel the light shift so many atoms can be interrogated Doppler- and recoil-free) that was predicted, realised and then reproduced at the 10^-18 level by independent laboratories with Sr, Yb and Hg, and that now yields physics (gravitational redshift over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants). The citation is narrow enough to stay distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes. Residual priority questions (Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hollberg) remain but do not outweigh the maturity and breadth of the case. P002 is a well-confirmed theoretical prediction but overlaps the 2016 topological-defect prize and has a system-dependent experimental record, so it is a distinct second; I still prefer it to no award.
recusal_note: Long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and co-author with Lund and ETH attosecond groups; I am also an atomic theorist working on precision calculations. No apparent connection to Katori or Ye, or to Young, Halperin or Nelson, so no recusal apparent from profile.
